Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans

post-traumatic muscle mass · peripheral ossification · motion and function

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • After a muscle contusion, a painful intramuscular mass with lost motion suggests myositis ossificans (post-traumatic heterotopic ossification). Symptoms can persist or worsen after 2 to 4 weeks; a pain-free interval may occur.
  • A film showing peripheral ossification within muscle, separate from bone supports it. Start with gentle range of motion and symptom relief; refer an atypical or enlarging mass before biopsy.
  • Rapidly worsening pain, spreading redness or systemic illness means possible necrotizing infection: urgent surgical assessment and antibiotics.
What it is

Benign bone formation in soft tissue, often in the quadriceps or brachialis

Driver

Muscle injury inflammation bone-forming cells; the proposed mechanism is fibroblast-to-osteoblast differentiation

Triggers

A direct sporting injury; may also follow surgery

Brain or spinal cord injury; less often stroke: a neurogenic form (non-modifiable)

Chain

Injured muscle an ossifying mass stiffness and restricted adjacent-joint motion

Insights

Movement helps localize it. Knee flexion can reproduce pain at a quadriceps mass.

The tissue matters. A muscular lesion separate from cortex favors this process over an osteosarcoma.

What the disease does, by systemSupporting detail
MuscleA firm, painful intramuscular massOssification limits movement nearby
Blood testsAlkaline phosphatase is often raised; inflammatory markers can be elevatedResults are nonspecific; assess infection from the clinical findings
Inherited disorderAn autosomal dominant progressive form is associated with an activin-receptor mutationKeep that inherited disorder distinct from an isolated mass after a contusion
2Urgent risks
InfectionSevere pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema or a toxic patient

If necrotizing infection is suspected, choose urgent surgery plus broad antibiotic treatment; do not delay for imaging.

TumorA growing or fixed mass, or an uncertain diagnosis

If malignancy is a concern, choose MRI with contrast and orthopedic oncology referral; the treating team plans the biopsy.

3Differential
Pain and a mass after a thigh injury
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Myositis ossificans (post-traumatic heterotopic ossification)A localized, firm mass after a muscle injury; motion hurtsWeeks after injury; peripheral calcification in muscle, separated from the cortex
Osteosarcoma An adolescent with persistent bone pain or swelling near a metaphysisA bone-centered lesion; investigate a growing or suspicious mass
Necrotizing soft-tissue infectionPain out of proportion, spreading red swollen tissue; systemic illnessRapid progression; immediate surgical assessment and antibiotics
Quadriceps tendon ruptureCannot actively extend the knee; a gap above the patellaA low patella with an extensor-mechanism deficit; surgical repair
Venous thrombosis Swelling involves the thigh and calf rather than a discrete muscle massVenous duplex identifies the clot
Osteoid osteomaNight pain improves with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID); no muscular massA bone lesion rather than peripheral muscle ossification
Neurogenic heterotopic ossificationPainful restricted joint after brain or spinal cord injury; less often strokeThe neurologic history and joint findings support the neurogenic form
4Workup
Clues that change the next step
CluePoints toNext best step
A stable mass with an early normal filmEvolving intramuscular ossification remains possibleReassess and repeat imaging at follow-up
A growing or uncertain massPossible tumorMRI and specialist-planned biopsy assessment
Cannot actively extend the knee; a gap above the patellaQuadriceps tendon ruptureArrange surgical repair

Pause point. A prior injury is tempting reassurance. A growing or uncertain mass still needs imaging and specialist review; the absence of fever or weight loss does not by itself exclude a sarcoma.

5Diagnostic criteria
Findings that support the diagnosis
FindingMeaning
Pain and motion may worsen after about 2 to 4 weeksCompatible with the developing ossified lesion
Radiographs can show the lesion at 3 to 4 weeksA normal earlier film is not definitive
Peripheral zonal ossification in muscleA nonmalignant ossification pattern; assess the entire lesion
6Severity
What changes management
FindingDo
Pain or loss of joint motionGentle rehabilitation and symptom relief
Persistent disabling symptomsOrthopedic assessment for further treatment
Systemic illness or rapid progressionUse the urgent infection branch in step 2
7Treatment
1

Conservativean established, typical post-traumatic lesion

Gentle range-of-motion exercise; an NSAID for symptomsAcute contusionFor a fresh contusion, ice and activity restriction come first. Gentle, static stretching starts no earlier than 48 hours after injury; acetaminophen is initially favored because an NSAID can increase bleeding. This differs from treating an established ossified lesion weeks later.
2

Reassesspain or restricted movement persists

Re-examine, review imaging and refer if function remains limited
3

Excisiona mature lesion remains symptomatic despite conservative care

Consider surgical excision; persistent lesions may be considered after 6 to 12 months
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
At reassessmentCheck pain, knee motion and the mass; repeat imaging when the initial film was early
The mass enlarges or remains uncertainRefer for MRI and a specialist diagnosis
During rehabilitationAvoid forceful stretching or deep massage; use gentle motion
Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy, football thigh contusion 4 weeks ago pain gone by 2 weeks, back last week indurated, mobile 3-cm anterior mass; no erythema passive knee flexion hurts; strength, sensation normal Vital signs normal · thigh girth +2 cm · pulses, calves normal → Myositis ossificans → injury, recovery, then pain with a mobile intramuscular mass weeks later, hurt by stretching the muscle: heterotopic bone; the localized post-traumatic course favors myositis ossificans; rapidly progressive pain or systemic illness needs urgent infection assessment, and an enlarging or uncertain mass needs tumor evaluation
  2. 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with myositis ossificans of the quadriceps today kicked in the thigh 4 weeks ago firm mass; knee flexion limited to 90 degrees Pain limits running Afebrile · radiograph: peripheral calcification → Range-of-motion exercise with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug → range of motion and an NSAID such as indomethacin; consider surgical assessment for a mature lesion with persistent symptoms
  3. 15-year-old girl with a firm thigh mass 3 weeks after a soccer collision mass unchanged in size over 1 week pain on passive knee flexion No night pain, weight loss or fever Vital signs normal · radiograph of the thigh normal → Repeat radiographs at follow-up → an early film may not show ossification; reassess and repeat radiographs for a typical stable lesion, while an enlarging or uncertain mass needs MRI and specialist review before biopsy
  4. 16-year-old boy with 1 day of severe thigh pain after a minor scrape spreading erythema and swelling pain out of proportion to the examination Confused and ill appearing T 39.0 °C · HR 128/min · BP 92/54 mm Hg → Emergency surgical exploration with broad-spectrum antibiotics → fever, spreading erythema and pain out of proportion within a day: necrotizing infection; operate now with broad antibiotics
  5. 45-year-old man who stumbled on stairs, landing on a flexed knee cannot extend the knee against gravity palpable gap just above the patella No induration or mass Sensation normal · knee radiograph: low-lying patella → Orthopedic referral for surgical repair → lost knee extension with a gap above the patella is a complete quadriceps tendon tear: surgical repair; the loss of active extension with a tendon gap distinguishes this tear from a post-traumatic intramuscular mass
  6. 24-year-old man 8 weeks after a traumatic brain injury stiff, painful right hip hard mass near the joint No fall or new injury since admission Afebrile · white cell count normal · alkaline phosphatase elevated → Neurogenic heterotopic ossification → Heterotopic ossification is a recognized complication after moderate or severe traumatic brain injury.
  7. 18-year-old man with quadriceps myositis ossificans diagnosed 12 months ago still painful; knee flexion limited despite range-of-motion therapy and NSAIDs Mass unchanged for 6 months Afebrile · radiograph: mature, well-defined bone → Surgical excision → a mature lesion that stays symptomatic is excised; surgical assessment is considered for a mature lesion with persistent symptoms
  8. 15-year-old boy was diagnosed with quadriceps myositis ossificans this week thigh contusion 3 weeks ago firm, tender anterior mass Asks how to speed recovery before the season Afebrile · knee flexion to 100 degrees → Aggressive passive stretching and deep massage of the lesion → Vigorous stretching may aggravate the condition. Avoid massaging the injured area; use gentle motion and symptom relief.

Transferable rule

A post-traumatic intramuscular mass with restricted motion and peripheral ossification suggests myositis ossificans. Persistent growth or an uncertain diagnosis needs imaging and specialist review.
